TESS archival follow-up · 18-19 October 2026 · conditional results, nothing validated

Three TESS candidates: TIC 270573718, TIC 262843927, TIC 193718989

A skeptical, reproducible re-examination of three long-period signals from the S1 survey batch 1, using every accessible local product and public archive. No new observing epoch exists for any of them: no TESS sector after 98 contains these stars, so every result below re-reduces the discovery photons or tests them against external catalogues and ground photometry.

Retain in the second tier. Timing structure unresolved.

TIC 270573718. The earlier “corrected 0.29 versus aperture 8.19” contradiction reproduces exactly and is not a disagreement between data products. Only the corrected series' early half spans 2018 and 2020. Its fitted period drift of -3.85 min per cycle, extrapolated over 45 cycles, moves the predicted late transits off the real ones. At the reference ephemeris the late events give S/N 7.25 (corrected) and 8.24 (aperture). Underneath it is a season-level timing pattern. All six 2020-21 transits arrive about 50-64 min early in every reduction, including two independent pixel extractions. Strictly periodic injections into the same data never produce that much coherence (tail p ≈ 0.04 per reduction). A free-shape fit with physically bounded shapes reproduces the early 2020-21 arrival in both PDCSAP and pixel data (unbounded, it is weaker in PDCSAP and unstable in the pixel series). Heavy-tailed timing errors still keep the protocol's claim rule from being met, so a transit-timing variation is suggestive, not established. With the season offsets removed, the transit is flat-bottomed and consistent with the catalogue density. The grazing, e ≈ 0.87 alternative was largely a product of folding misaligned transits. The high nearby-source FPP is reconciled: injection-calibrated difference images exclude every catalogued neighbour that TRICERATOPS weighted, and this holds with a deliberately broadened PRF.

TIC 262843927. Sectors 31 and 88 failed because the star was off the CCD's science pixels (CCD columns about 2112 and 31, outside 45-2092). Nothing there can be salvaged, and nothing there is a non-detection. The transit shape is central (b ≈ 0.2-0.4) at the catalogue density. Undiluted brown-dwarf or stellar occultors, and equal twins at 2P, are disfavoured by Δχ² ≈ 10.6-11.3 and would need e ≈ 0.9. Gaia's RV constancy over 23 epochs limits a companion to the target to M sin i < 20-28 MJ. The reported NFPP = 0 holds only for small apertures. In a 3-pixel aperture two wide neighbours could supply the depth, so the protection comes from the image test, not the flux budget. Two findings weigh against it. The star sits about 0.2 mag above the single-star sequence for its colour, and it also shows Gaia astrometric excess noise (15.2σ) and RUWE 1.31, so an unresolved companion carrying roughly 15-20% of the light is likely. That would raise the radius about 10% if the transit is on the primary, or move it to the companion. Its 24.11-d signal also ranked only ninth in its own search (stitch S/N 8.86), although Stage C's blind search ranked it first.

TIC 193718989. The 9.8″ neighbour would need an 83-90% eclipse with the actual PRF throughput, beyond what a main-sequence pair can produce. ZTF DR24 detects it at normal brightness inside the predicted eclipse window at both period parities, and the calibrated image test disfavours it. The “4.91 versus 2.31” statistic was again a drift extrapolation driven by one partly covered 2020 event. The shape is planet-like but only mildly disfavours eccentric grazing brown dwarfs (Δχ² 2.4-4.9), and Gaia RVs allow companions up to 70-124 MJ.

Luminosity for colour. Against 71,717 Gaia stars within 100 pc, only TIC 262843927 is over-luminous for its colour (about 0.2 mag). TIC 270573718 and TIC 193718989 sit on or slightly below the single-star sequence. The test cannot see companions fainter than about 2-2.5 mag (details).

Across all three. Public archival work has reached diminishing returns. The remaining alternatives (unresolved companions inside about 1-2″, diluted or eccentric eclipsing systems that fit the shape, and for 270 the timing question) need new observations. The smallest useful ones are named in the synthesis.

Inputs, provenance and the frozen protocol

Both prior reports were read in full: SEVEN CANDIDATES / CONTINUATION AUDIT (26 pp., Codex bundle continue-the-seven-candidate-tess-analysis) and THREE TESS CANDIDATES / Further archival constraints (22 pp.). The 22-page report was not attached to the request; it was found after the protocol freeze in .claude\tess_three_audit. It concerns TIC 382098683, 188830138 and 201247574, the current top tier, and supplied the QLP and TGLC product caveats and the TRICERATOPS source audit used here. The original batch-1 deep-vetting report (19 pp.) and its bundle were also read. The prior numbers quoted in the request were verified against those bundles. Every value checked reproduces, including the 0.29 / 8.19, 4.91 / 2.31 and 9.09 / 4.11 retrospective statistics, which were recomputed with the continuation's own code. The request described one point imprecisely: the TIC 270573718 “aperture” series is the survey's Stage-D TESScut 1-pixel aperture in eight sectors, not a freshly extracted series.

Discovery code: repository commit df39814a9936 (branch s1/survey), preset survey_k1: periods 0.5-50 d, durations 0.02-0.35 d in 14 log steps, sectors ≤ 98 at native cadence, at least 3 transits, an 8,100-s search budget, then pre-gate, Stage A, S (bound_alias), B, C and D. All inputs were opened read-only and hashed (manifests/input_manifest.csv; 41 groups). The analysis protocol was frozen at 2026-10-18T21:08:37Z (SHA-256 dd9f219ff2ecec63…) before any post-discovery epoch was looked for. Four amendments are recorded in the file: A1 (report found; TGLC and free-shape timing added), A2 (post-hoc: the empirical timing null, a neighbour-selection fix and an RV-statistic fix), A3 (a bounded free-shape timing variant, a read-only tabulation of the discovery funnel, and the replay's summary statistics, fixed before any injected search had run) and A4 (the colour-magnitude over-luminosity check, added at the reader's request).

Times are BTJD = BJDTDB − 2457000 throughout; ZTF times were converted from MJDUTC to BJDTDB at Palomar. The packet fit stores marginal errors at cycle 0 only (none for TIC 262843927, whose central-transit covariance is singular). The “frozen” column below is a conditional linear ephemeris refit to per-event times from the discovery products, with errors inflated by √χ²red, and fixed before any later data were searched.

Public-archive census

659 receipted requests (MAST, TESScut, TCE bulk files, ExoFOP, VizieR, Gaia TAP and DataLink, IRSA ZTF, ASAS-SN, LAMOST, RAVE, ESO, KOA, NASA Exoplanet Archive, SIMBAD and web search). Full notes and receipts are in results/census/.

  • No new epochs. MAST holds SPOC FFIs through S109, TICA through S107 and QLP through S104. No sector after 98 contains any of the three stars. TIC 193718989 next falls on silicon in S117-S119 (May-July 2027). TIC 270573718's S97 appears only in a TICA footprint and is off the SPOC footprint by 27 px. TIC 262843927's S31 and S88 are off the science pixels (pixel check below). The retrospective splits are therefore the only “recurrence” tests possible.
  • Other reductions of the same photons (sensitivity tests only): QLP, TARS, TGLC (fetched by direct path for sectors 1-55, which the MAST index omits), GSFC-ELEANOR-LITE, T16, TASOC. TIC 262843927 also has SPOC 2-min data in S1-S3.
  • Catalogues. No SPOC TCE in 57 single- and multi-sector files (only TIC 262843927 was ever a SPOC 2-min target, in S1-S3, where each sector holds at most two transits of low S/N). No TOI or CTOI within 2′. No match in seven TESS eclipsing-binary catalogues, ASAS-SN, ATLAS, ZTF periodic, WISE or CSS variables, or the Gaia DR3 eclipsing-binary and non-single-star tables. Absences are not treated as negative science.
  • Gaia DR3 flags. TIC 262843927: RUWE 1.31 and astrometric excess-noise significance 15.2, a hint of an unresolved companion. TIC 193718989: the Discrete Source Classifier returns P(binary star) = 0.999999; its reliability for single M dwarfs is not established here, so it is recorded as a flag only. TIC 270573718 and 193718989 are flagged VARIABLE (SOLAR_LIKE). No Gaia source lies within 5″ of any target.
  • Spectroscopy. TIC 262843927 has two RAVE velocities (7.5 ± 2.0 and 3.1 ± 3.5 km/s) consistent with Gaia (8.25 ± 0.51). TIC 193718989 has one LAMOST DR11 spectrum (dM0, about −7.4 ± 2.0 km/s) consistent with Gaia (−5.44 ± 1.07). No high-resolution imaging or contrast curve exists for any target.
  • Gaia epochs. Gaia DR3 epoch photometry, the only pre-TESS time series (36 epochs for TIC 270573718, 46 for TIC 193718989, 2014-2017), has no epoch within ±3σ of a predicted transit; TIC 262843927 has no Gaia epoch photometry.
  • Ground time series. ZTF DR24 (TIC 193718989 and eight neighbours within 60″; the 9.8″ star has 2081 clean detections). ZTF and ATLAS forced photometry need accounts and were not used. ASAS-SN light curves were unavailable (service down since 13 October 2026).
  • Access failures (not negative results): every ExoFOP per-target endpoint returns the literal body “Array” with HTTP 200 (the bulk TOI/CTOI tables do download); the NASA Exoplanet Archive cone search was blocked by Cloudflare (403).
  • Product caveats. The QLP S99-S104 timing error affects none of these stars. The QLP S74-S79 fix touches only TIC 193718989's S79 file, which is the corrected v02 and was not used by discovery.
  • Prior public analysis. TIC 193718989 is a candidate in github.com/eumemic/exoplanets (added 2026-10-08): P = 24.5329228 d, Rp 2.58 R⊕, TRICERATOPS FPP 0.029 (0.011 with Gaia/MOLUSC constraints). It uses the same TESS-SPOC photons and is not independent confirmation, but it matters for novelty and attribution.

Methods common to all three targets

Events. An event is admitted by coverage only (at least half the in-transit interval sampled, at least 3 in-transit and 4 baseline bins on each side). It is never admitted by its fitted sign. Each admitted event gets a signed depth from a fixed-shape, exposure-integrated batman template with a local linear baseline (quadratic as a check). Errors are white out-of-transit scatter times a time-averaging β factor, and pooled errors are inflated by √χ²red.

Reductions of the same photons. The discovery input (biweight-flattened); the same TESS-SPOC/QLP flux with local baselines; pipeline SAP; the survey's Stage-D TESScut aperture; TGLC aperture and PSF; and nine predeclared FU3 TESScut extractions (radius 1.0, 1.5 and 2.0 px circles and a neighbour-excluding aperture, each with an annulus or a plane sky, plus PRF scene photometry, run only when the scene residual is at most 10% of the target peak). These are sensitivity tests, never independent detections.

Calibration. Injections at shifted epochs with the real transits masked measure depth and timing errors per cadence group. Random null epochs measure how often a single epoch shows a dip as deep as the median real event. For timing, strictly periodic copies of the transit were injected at 24 phases and timed with the identical method. This showed heavy-tailed timing errors that a robust-scatter calibration underestimates.

Host tests. Per-pixel transit-decrement maps are pooled per sector, with empirical per-pixel noise from 48 off-transit control maps. The tested sources are the target, every Gaia source within 2.5 px or brighter than Gtarget + 6 within 4 px, every TRICERATOPS nearby-scenario host, and every neighbour the flux budget finds capable in a 1.5-3 px aperture. Each is scored by a non-negative PRF amplitude fit. The score is calibrated by injecting the dip into the real cubes on the target and on each neighbour, using both the mission PRF and a PRF broadened by a 0.35-px Gaussian.

Flux budget. Gaia G/BP/RP give TESS magnitudes (Stassun et al. 2019). Mission-PRF throughput in apertures of 1.5-3 px gives the eclipse depth each neighbour would need. A main-sequence pair removes at most about 50% of its light, and an unresolved contaminant must lie within ΔT = −2.5 log10(depth/fmax).

Physical models. Profile-likelihood and MCMC shape fits use per-event baselines profiled analytically, with (k, b, ρeff), an optional dilution and optional per-season timing offsets. The minimum eccentricity follows from ρeff/ρ★ (Dawson & Johnson 2012). Gaia DR3 RV constancy statistics were converted to companion-mass limits with a relative Monte Carlo statistic. TRICERATOPS scenario weights come from the continuation's four existing runs and 27 prior reweightings; no new draws were made.

TIC 270573718 · P = 41.3837 d

Bottom line. A real, repeating dip in the discovery data on the named target, with all catalogued neighbours excluded as hosts by the calibrated image test. Its nature is unresolved. It is classified under protocol rule 5.7 as (ii) persistent astrophysical dip, host and nature not resolved. It is not (i), a processing artefact, because the dip is present in every target-centred raw-pixel extraction. It is not (iii), planet-favoured, because binary alternatives are disfavoured by Δχ² of only 8.4 (PDCSAP) and 2.2 (pixel series), short of the predeclared 10.

(a) Initial claim and checked provenance

Packet fit: P = 41.383701 ± 0.000101 d, T0 = BTJD 1334.9038, T14 = 3.76 h, R★ = 0.463 R☉ (TIC; Gaia GSP-Phot gives 0.509). The discovery used 23 sectors: TESS-SPOC PDCSAP at 1800 s (S1-S11), 600 s (S27-S37) and 200 s (S61-S68), and QLP det_flux at 200 s (S87-S98). Of 16 predicted events, 15 are admitted. S95's event is fully quality-flagged in QLP. The QLP files are v01 and are not among the sectors with documented timing errors.

The contradiction, decomposed (s01_270_reproduce.py): the continuation's own code reproduces 0.2927 and 8.1926 exactly. Of the two series, only the corrected one has early events from 2018 (S1, S4, S5, S7) as well as 2020 (S27-S33). The aperture series' early half is S5, S27, S33 and S65. The corrected early fit finds a period correction of -3.85 min per cycle, robust to dropping any single early sector (S/N 0.27-0.74). Extrapolated to cycles 22-65, it shifts the predicted late transits by 1-4 h. On a common event set the corrected value rises to 3.63. With an epoch-only early fit it is 7.79, and at the reference ephemeris 7.25. The aperture series gives 8.24 at the reference ephemeris. The two reductions agree; the statistic does not, because it extrapolates a drift that the data constrain poorly.

Timing. Per-event mid-times were measured in nine reductions. All of them show the same seasonal pattern relative to the reference ephemeris: 2018 ≈ +8 min, 2020-21 ≈ −50 to −64 min, 2023 ≈ +20-37 min, 2024-25 ≈ +3 to +13 min. The pipeline products, SAP, the survey TESScut aperture, TGLC aperture and PSF, and the FU3 pixel series all agree. A timestamp control rules out the FFI clock. WASP-62 b, in the same southern-CVZ cameras, has TESS-SPOC 600-s FFI transit times that match its SPOC 2-min times to within 0.16 to 0.60 min in each 2020-21 sector.

Significance depends on the error model. With formal errors, a linear ephemeris fails badly (χ² 91.8/13). Injection-calibrated errors reduce this to 53.5 (adopted shape) or 25.4 (grazing shape). Strictly periodic injections into the same light curve, timed identically, reveal heavy-tailed errors: the null season Δχ² reaches up to 123, so the observed 86.2 has tail p = 0.08. Coherence is a different matter. The largest season-median offset in any null run is 18 min (PDCSAP), against 64 min observed with 6/6 events sharing the sign (tail p 0.04; similar in SAP and the pixel series). Under the predeclared rule (section 4: Δχ² ≥ 11.8 after inflation, the same pattern in an independent extraction, survival of leave-one-out), the timing variation is not established. The grazing-calibrated leave-one-out minimum is 9.5 once S34 is dropped.

Free-shape cross-check. Each event was refitted with a trapezoid whose depth, duration and ingress are free (amendment A1). Unbounded, the PDCSAP fit weakens the pattern (2020-21 season offset −28 min, event median −39 min, 4 of 6 events early). In the unclipped pixel series the unbounded fit latches onto outliers: the S1 fit is a 25-ppt, 1.1-h feature at the duration bound, so its +108-min 2018 offset is not interpreted. A post-hoc bounded variant (A3: depth 0-3× adopted, duration 0.6-1.6× adopted, isolated 5σ points removed from each window) gives the 2020-21 season about 50 min early with all six events sharing the sign in both series. The season pattern is therefore not an artefact of the fixed template. Its significance still rests on the injection null (p ≈ 0.04), which was computed for the template method only, and the 2023 and 2024-25 offsets differ between methods by up to 30 min.

(c) Primary-signal reliability and selection limits

All 15 admitted events are positive in the pipeline products, and 14-15 of 15 in every FU3 pixel extraction. Pooled S/N is 8-12 and depths are consistent across events (pconst 0.02-0.47). Random null epochs reach the median event depth in 0.5% (PDCSAP) to 2.8% (SAP) of trials. No event lies within 0.8 d of a segment edge or near a momentum dump or scattered-light flag. These are all re-reductions of the discovery photons. Discovery selected the period and these events, and no later epoch exists. The selection replay is in the Selection replay section.

(d) Host attribution

The difference images tested 10 sources across 15 sectors. For every neighbour with a calibrated neighbour-hosted injection set, the observed summed Δχ² lies above the 95th percentile of that set, under the mission PRF and the broadened PRF alike (8 of 8 excluded). Each observed value falls inside the target-hosted injection range. The 34.4″ G = 14.71 star needs only a 1% eclipse and carried most of the nearby-source FPP. Its observed score is 76.5, against a neighbour-hosted distribution centred near -382.

The earlier “conflict” between image tests and FPP is explained. TRICERATOPS computes NFPP from each neighbour's flux share in the aperture and never uses where the dimming sits in the image. Removing only the nearby scenarios whose hosts the image test excludes (TICs 270573715, 270573719, 270573720, 270573722) moves the FPP from 21.5%-45.7% to 3.5%-9.1%, and NFPP to 0.0007-0.0027. This is a conditional sensitivity bound, not a joint posterior. The image test and the light curve share photons, and the image test is calibrated only for the PRF family and perturbation tested. Unresolved companions within a few arcseconds behave like the target in these maps and remain open. Gaia RUWE is 1.12, and Gaia finds no source within 5″.

(e) Planet versus binary and brown-dwarf alternatives

Folded on a linear ephemeris, the transit looks V-shaped (best b = 0.95, ρeff 0.34 versus 6.52 g cm-3). That shape is what allowed the earlier e ≈ 0.87 grazing companion and the 2P twins to fit as well as a planet. Freeing one timing offset per season improves the fit by Δχ² = 50 for four parameters and gives a flat-bottomed central transit: b = 0.15, ρeff = 9.19, catalogue density acceptable at Δχ² 0.2. Large occultors (k ≥ 0.3 diluted, or undiluted 0.08-0.20 R☉ bodies needing e ≥ 0.81) are then disfavoured by Δχ² 8.4 in PDCSAP but only 2.2 in the noisier pixel series. The shape argument therefore rests on the timing offsets being real, and is not independent evidence for them.

Odd and even depths agree within 1.2σ in all nine reductions, which says nothing against equal twins. A 0.52 ± 0.19 ppt dip at phase 0.5 appears in PDCSAP (phase-shift null p = 0.003). It falls to 0.35 in SAP and to 0.02-0.26 in the FU3 pixel series (p ≥ 0.07). It is not a robust secondary eclipse. If it were real it would require an eclipsing star, because no 2 R⊕ planet at 41 d produces a 0.5 ppt occultation. Gaia publishes no RV-constancy test at this brightness, so there is no RV limit.

(f) Model and prior sensitivity

Conditional on the named target hosting an undiluted transit, with the season offsets free: Rp = 2.31 [2.05, 2.60] R⊕ (68 %; density free), 2.25 [2.01, 2.50] R⊕ (circular orbit at the catalogue density); b = 0.57 [0.20, 0.82] / 0.46 [0.23, 0.63]; P(b > 0.8) = 0.20 / 0.02. Without the offsets the geometry is grazing-ambiguous and the radius is poorly bounded. TRICERATOPS (four runs, 27 prior reweightings each) gives package FPP 21.5%-45.7%, NFPP 0.187-0.438, target-host planet weight 54.3%-78.5% and any-host planet-label weight 61.5%-85.8%. Prior reweighting alone spans 1.1-98.6% FPP. None of these is a probability that a planet exists.

(g) What changed since the prior reports

  • The 0.29 / 8.19 contradiction is resolved: a drift extrapolation plus different event sets, not inconsistent reductions.
  • New: a season-coherent timing structure in nine reductions, not produced by strictly periodic injections and not a clock error, but short of the claim rule.
  • New: the grazing / e ≈ 0.87 and 2P-twin shape solutions are largely produced by timing smearing. With the offsets removed, the shape is central and planet-like.
  • New: calibrated difference images exclude every catalogued neighbour behind the 19-44% NFPP.
  • Unchanged: no new epoch exists, no RV constraint, and the half-phase dip is not robust.

(h) Viable, disfavoured and excluded-only-under-assumptions

  • Viable: a sub-Neptune on the target (Rp ≈ 2.2-2.3 R⊕), possibly with transit-timing variations from a non-transiting companion; a planet on an unresolved bound companion (STP); a diluted eclipsing pair within a few arcseconds with a small radius ratio; an eclipsing pair in a hierarchical triple whose timing variations match the pattern.
  • Disfavoured: an undiluted grazing brown dwarf or low-mass star on the target needing e ≥ 0.8, and equal twins at 82.77 d, but only if the season offsets are real (Δχ² 2-8).
  • Excluded only under stated assumptions: eclipses on any catalogued neighbour (mission and broadened PRF, real-cube injections); a light-travel-time explanation of the timing pattern (a ±40-min amplitude over about 5 yr needs a companion of several solar masses).

(i) Further public-data work

Little remains. Re-reductions agree, and a TESS clock error is excluded. Further reprocessing of the same photons would not test the timing structure. The next informative data are a resolved ground or space transit at the predicted epoch with a window of at least ±2 h (linear-ephemeris 1σ ≈ 7 min near the reference epoch, larger with drift), which would measure the next O−C and the shape. RV monitoring would test stellar-mass companions.

TIC 262843927 · P = 24.1089 d

Bottom line. The cleanest of the three. The dip is real in the discovery data, and every catalogued neighbour is excluded as host by the calibrated image test. The shape is a central transit at the catalogue density, and Gaia RVs exclude stellar and heavy brown-dwarf companions to the target. What remains is the generic unresolved-companion family (planet or eclipsing pair on a star within about 1-2″), which Gaia's astrometric excess noise leaves plausible. Recommendation: join the top follow-up tier.

(a) Initial claim and checked provenance

Packet fit: P = 24.108929 d, T0 = BTJD 1332.7877, T14 = 3.71 h, b ≈ 0. No formal P or T0 error exists because the covariance is singular at b = 0. The FU3 linear refit gives P = 24.108507 ± 0.000213 d. Discovery used 15 sectors: TESS-SPOC 1800 s (S1-S4), 600 s (S28-S34) and 200 s (S61-S69), and QLP 200 s (S95-S97). The “early-to-late 9.09 versus 4.11” difference is a noise difference, not a timing effect: at the reference ephemeris the late halves give 8.75 (corrected) and 4.27 (the survey's smaller, noisier TESScut aperture), and the early fits imply negligible drift.

Sectors 31 and 88 (s09_262_s31_s88.py). Through the cutout WCS the star falls on CCD column 2112.2 (S31, camera 4 CCD 2) and 31.3 (S88, camera 4 CCD 3). Both lie outside the science columns 45-2092, in the virtual overclock and underclock regions. The median image at the target position is 0.01 and 0.34 e-/s, against about 845 e-/s expected for a T = 12.0 star. tess-point agrees that the star was not on silicon, and no pipeline light curve exists for either sector. The prior “gross failures” were geometric. No repair is possible, and these sectors are neither detections nor non-detections.

(d) Host attribution

The reported NFPP = 0 came from TRICERATOPS's admission rule: no catalogued neighbour can make the 1.2 ppt dip in its aperture. That is true in small apertures. In the FU3 1.5-px aperture the nearest capable neighbour would need more than a 100% eclipse. In a 3-px aperture, two wide stars could supply it (65″, ΔT 3.9, about 9%; 103″, ΔT 1.9, about 20%). The calibrated image test settles this. All 5 tested sources score ΣΔχ² +42 to +62 over 14 sectors, inside the target-hosted injection range. Every neighbour-hosted injection set lies far below, for both PRF versions (5 of 5 excluded).

The open family is unresolved companions. Gaia DR3 gives RUWE 1.31 and an astrometric excess-noise significance of 15.2, which is suggestive of a companion but not proof. TRICERATOPS's residual FPP is almost entirely STP (a planet on an unresolved bound companion). An unresolved eclipsing contaminant must have ΔT ≤ 7.19 (≤ 6.44 for a main-sequence pair). No contrast curve exists.

Large occultors are disfavoured: diluted k ≥ 0.3 at Δχ² 10.6, undiluted 0.08-0.20 R☉ bodies at 10.6-11.3, which would need e ≥ 0.89. The phase-0.5 depth is -0.017 ± 0.093 ppt (PDCSAP). A circular eclipsing binary at P would therefore need a secondary below about 0.17 ppt, roughly 14% of the primary, which requires a companion much cooler than the eclipsed star. The earlier 2-ppt secondary-search sensitivity could not constrain diluted eclipses of this depth at all. Gaia RV constancy (23 transits, p = 0.977) limits a companion to the target, for the named target as host: M sin i < 20 MJ (circular, P), 22 (e = 0.8), 25-28 at 2P. This excludes stellar and heavy brown-dwarf occultors on the target. It says nothing about a blended pair, whose lines would not move the target's.

(g) What changed since the prior reports

  • The S31/S88 failures are explained as off-silicon geometry, not PRF, noise or crowding problems.

(h) Viable, disfavoured and excluded-only-under-assumptions

  • Viable: a 1.9-2.0 R⊕ planet on the target in a low-eccentricity orbit; a planet on an unresolved bound companion (STP, favoured by the astrometric noise if the companion is real); a diluted eclipsing pair with a small radius ratio on a star within about 1-2″.
  • Disfavoured: grazing or eccentric brown dwarfs and low-mass stars on the target (shape Δχ² ≈ 11, RV); diluted pairs with radius ratio ≥ 0.3, including equal twins at 2P (Δχ² ≈ 11).
  • Excluded only under stated assumptions: any catalogued neighbour as host (mission and broadened PRF injections); a companion to the target above about 20-28 MJ (Gaia RV error model).

(i) Further public-data work

Little remains. The SPOC 2-min S1-S3 light curves could refine the ingress shape slightly, but cover the same epochs. The decisive next data are high-resolution imaging (to test the companion that Gaia's excess noise hints at) and a ground transit with resolved photometry, followed by RVs.

Bottom line. The archival ground data and the blend analysis improve host attribution materially. The 9.8″ neighbour is disfavoured by three lines: it would need an 83-90% eclipse, ZTF sees it at normal brightness inside the eclipse window, and the calibrated image test favours the target. The planet interpretation is weaker than for TIC 262843927, because the transit shape only mildly disfavours eccentric grazing brown dwarfs and Gaia RVs allow companions up to about 70-124 MJ. (d) Host attribution: the 9.8″ neighbour and others

Flux budget. Gaia DR3 1346023547768414976 (G 19.59, BP−RP 1.85, 9.8″) has T ≈ 18.8, ΔT 6.4 from the target. With mission-PRF throughput it would need to lose 86% of its own light in the most favourable aperture and sector (0.83-0.90 across sectors with an RP-band flux ratio instead of T). That is beyond the roughly 50% a main-sequence pair can produce. The earlier 74% came from equal throughput and the RP band. TRICERATOPS assigned this star no weight, consistent with that physics.

ZTF DR24 (detections only; forced photometry is account-gated and was not used). The star has 2081 clean detections (zg 509, zr 1333, zi 239). Using the frozen ephemeris and its inflated covariance, propagated to each ZTF timestamp, 9 detections fall inside the nominal eclipse window, against 11.8 expected if the star never dims. There is no censoring deficit, although a deep eclipse would push it below the single-epoch limit. Two detections lie robustly inside the window even after a 3σ timing allowance. Both are even-parity cycles, at flux 0.935 ± 0.039 of normal, so any eclipse there is shallower than 13% (95%). Odd-parity detections 0.6-1.1 h from predicted mid-eclipse are also at normal brightness, apart from one 0.46-mag-faint point next to a normal one in the same visit. Of the grid of eclipse models (depth 50-100%, durations 0.8-1.2 T14, ±3σ timing), 97% are contradicted by at least one detection.

Image test. The observed ΣΔχ² for this star is 26.4. Target-hosted injections give a median of 19.7, and dips injected on the neighbour give a median of -30.5 (95th percentile -8.7; -6.2 with the broadened PRF). At 0.5 px separation the two hypotheses overlap more than for distant stars, so this line is the weakest of the three. The fitted single-source centroids scatter 2.5-9.3″ in directions unrelated to the neighbour (mean cosine about −0.05).

Across all 17 tested sources over 7 sectors, including the brighter stars at 65″ and 117″ that could supply the depth in large apertures, 12 of 12 with a neighbour-hosted injection set are excluded under both PRF versions. The rest are consistent with a target host. Remaining: unresolved companions within about 1-2″ (Gaia RUWE 1.04, no Gaia source within 5″, DSC binary flag recorded, no contrast curve).

Brown dwarfs around M dwarfs at 25-50 d are rare (the “desert”), and the grazing geometry occupies a small fraction of transiting orientations. These solutions exist geometrically but carry low prior weight. Two caveats: this is not a calibrated probability, and the Gaia RV limit does not reach them.

(i) Further public-data work

Little remains. ZTF forced photometry would extend the neighbour test to non-detections, but needs an account. Better is a resolved multiband transit, which measures the target's depth directly (the neighbour is 9.8″ away), followed by RVs reaching the brown-dwarf regime (K ≈ 1-7 km/s) and high-resolution imaging.

Discovery selection: the funnel and a bounded replay

The funnel that chose these signals. S1 batch 1 searched 2,000 stars. 1,476 stars produced at least one pre-gate candidate (4,655 in all). Stage A passed 141 of them on 77 stars (25 stars had two or more), Stages S and B passed 127 and 127, and Stage C's blind search passed 32, one per star. Review then kept 23 SUBMIT/HOLD stars, the earlier continuation took seven, and these three come from those seven. All three passed every stage. The table lists each pre-gate candidate on the three stars.

The unfavourable fact is TIC 262843927. Its 24.11-d signal ranked only ninth in its own search (stitch S/N 8.86, the lowest of the three), behind eight others on the same star, including several stronger but spurious ones. Two other periods on that star (14.52 d and 30.23 d) also passed Stages A, S and B and failed only at Stage C, because the blind TLS's strongest peak was at 106.67 d. For the 24.11-d candidate the blind TLS's strongest peak was the candidate itself (SDE 25.9). The light curve of this star is busy, and the signal was found near the search threshold. TIC 270573718 and TIC 193718989 were their stars' top-ranked signals.

The frozen search (survey.run_job, preset survey_k1, 8,100-s budget, identical pre-gate) and Stage A (funnel_k2.py, S mode bound_alias, C variant V3) were run in an isolated data root on fixed sets, chosen before any flux was read. The sets are the three targets' light curves with the sign inverted (dips become bumps), 24 inverted matched controls from batch 1 (same slice, |ΔTmag| ≤ 0.5, usable sectors within ±30%), and 24 other matched controls with each candidate's own transit injected by the frozen injection code at a random epoch. Limits: 24 CPU-h and 4 workers, with no extension. Finished 2026-10-19T05:57:50Z: 51 of 51 searches, 17.2 CPU-h used.

What this covers: the search's look-elsewhere space over 0.5-50 d, its grids, gaps and budget, and the pre-gate and Stage A cuts, on matched noise. What it does not cover: the S/B/C/D stages, the human/Codex review that picked seven of the 23 SUBMIT/HOLD stars, and batch-to-batch choices. Inverted light curves are only a partial null, because asymmetric systematics (PDC-made dips) do not invert symmetrically. The survey's own K1 calibration on 250 uninjected stars found 0.088 natural candidates per star surviving Stage S. Those are real-star false alarms (systematics, variables, binaries), not pure noise.

Null result. The 27 inverted light curves searched gave 68 pre-gate candidates, with stitch S/N up to 352.4, well above the three real candidates (8.9-10.4). Search S/N alone therefore does not separate these signals from noise. Stage A does: none of the 68 inverted candidates passed it. With 27 stars and no passes, the per-star rate of noise-only Stage A passes is below 11% (95%). That bound is too weak to make the batch's survivors secure by itself: at the bound, the 1,476 batch-1 stars with a pre-gate candidate could yield up to about 35 noise signals reaching Stage C (using the observed 23% Stage A→C survival of real-data passes, an assumption for noise), against 32 actual Stage C survivors. The replay shows that Stage A is not easily fooled by the same noise; each signal's security still rests on its own per-event and per-reduction evidence.

Recovery. TIC 270573718's transit was recovered through Stage A on 5 of 8 matched stars (pre-gate match 6 of 8); recovered stitch S/N median 8.2 against the real candidate's 9.91 (1 of 6 recoveries at or above it). TIC 262843927's transit was recovered through Stage A on 6 of 8 matched stars (pre-gate match 6 of 8); recovered stitch S/N median 8.1 against the real candidate's 8.86 (2 of 6 recoveries at or above it). TIC 193718989's transit was recovered through Stage A on 6 of 8 matched stars (pre-gate match 6 of 8); recovered stitch S/N median 11.8 against the real candidate's 10.40 (4 of 6 recoveries at or above it). Recovery of 5-6 in 8 means the search finds signals like these most of the time but not always. Each real candidate's discovery S/N lies inside the range its injections reached, so the replay shows no sign that the measured depths are strongly inflated by selection. With 8 injections per candidate this is a coarse check.

Twice-period and long-period checks (targeted; not part of the survey's look-elsewhere space): Stage C's blind TLS (0.5-110 d) already ranked P first for all three, with 2P peaks lower (TIC 270573718: 82.77 d at SDE 40.3 versus 58.2 at P; TIC 193718989: 49.07 d at SDE 16.4 versus 37.9). No long-period solution beats the reported period, and no 2P alias stands out where odd/even depths agree. After the candidate's transits are masked, no residual peak exceeds SDE about 7. Is each star over-luminous for its colour?

An unresolved companion of similar brightness lifts a star above the single-star main sequence at its colour. An equal-mass pair sits 0.75 mag above it, a companion 1.5 mag fainter about 0.24 mag above, and one 3 mag fainter only 0.07 mag above. This check was added at the reader's request (amendment A4). Each target was placed on four empirical colour-magnitude diagrams built from Gaia DR3 stars within 100 pc (71,717 after the BP/RP flux-excess cut), with 2MASS Ks from Gaia's own cross-match. The reference is the single-star ridge, the most common absolute magnitude at each colour among 44,312 clean stars (RUWE < 1.2, no Gaia binary solution, no multi-peak flag). Metallicity spreads single stars around that ridge, and the spread measured from the same clean stars is given below. Extinction is neglected at 85 pc.

TIC 262843927 is mildly over-luminous in all four diagrams (ΔM -0.17 to -0.23 mag). Only 11%-17% of clean stars at its colour are as bright. On its own that is inside the single-star spread, because a metal-rich single star can sit there. It does not stand alone. This is also the only target with an elevated RUWE (1.31) and a significant astrometric excess noise (15.2σ), and those measure the image's motion and shape, not its brightness. Together they make an unresolved companion the most economical reading, though not a proven one. If the primary sits on the ridge, the companion is about 1.5-1.9 mag fainter in G and carries 14%-19% of the light. An equal-mass pair is disfavoured but not excluded: 10%-19% of clean single stars at this colour are faint enough to make one look like this star. The consequences for the transit are as follows. If it is on the primary, the depth is diluted and the radius rises by about 8-11% (up to about 41% for an equal pair). If it is on the companion, the undiluted depth is about 6-8 ppt on an M2-M3 dwarf, a body of roughly 3-4 R⊕. The transit duration's agreement with the primary's density would then be a coincidence. The diluted-pair cases are already inside the dilution-free k-profiles. High-resolution imaging, already the recommended first observation for this star, tests the companion directly.

TIC 270573718 and TIC 193718989 are not over-luminous. TIC 270573718 sits slightly below the ridge (ΔM +0.11 to +0.25 mag) and TIC 193718989 on it (+0.01 to +0.04 mag). Both have RUWE near 1 and no astrometric excess noise. An equal-mass pair would need the primary to lie in the faintest 4%-12% of single stars at those colours (5% or less in the three diagrams with the narrower single-star spread). For TIC 193718989 this does not support Gaia's DSC “binary” probability (0.999999), which is derived from the low-resolution spectra rather than the colour-magnitude position.

Limit. The test cannot see companions more than about 2-2.5 mag fainter in G, because their lift (< 0.1-0.15 mag) is inside the single-star spread. Those faint companions are the ones that matter for most blended-eclipse scenarios, so a normal colour-magnitude position does not exclude them.

TIC 270573718HIGHMODERATELOWTiming structure (TTV versus eclipsing pair in a triple versus noise); diluted pair; STPRetain, second tier. A transit with a ≥±2 h window measures the next O−C and the shape; RVs.

The confidence labels are qualitative and conditional on the stated assumptions: Gaia completeness outside about 1-2″, the mission-PRF family with the tested perturbation, main-sequence physics for blended pairs, and the Gaia RV error model. They are not probabilities. “Repeating dip: HIGH” means present in 5-9 re-reductions of the discovery photons with low null false-dip rates. No independent epoch exists, and the replay is reported separately.

Should TIC 262843927 or TIC 193718989 join the top tier? Both should. TIC 262843927 has the strongest planet-versus-binary case of the three: a planet-like central shape at the catalogue density, and RVs that exclude stellar and heavy brown-dwarf companions to the target. Its host case is weaker than first stated. The star is about 0.2 mag over-luminous for its colour and has significant astrometric excess noise, so an unresolved companion is likely, and the transit could be on it. Its signal was also found near the search threshold. TIC 193718989 has the cleaner host case: no sign of a companion, and its 9.8″ neighbour is excluded (its host attribution is now about as good as 201247574's in the prior report). Its planet-versus-brown-dwarf separation is weaker. 262 keeps a narrow lead because a companion would change its radius and host star, not its planetary character, whereas 193's brown-dwarf alternative would remove the planet. The order between the two is close.

TIC 270573718: retain, downgrade below both. It should not be dropped, because the dip is real in the discovery data, its host is the target among catalogued stars, and the earlier contradiction and NFPP conflict are both resolved. Its planet interpretation depends on whether the season timing structure is real. If it is, the shape favours a small central transiter and the system may be dynamically interesting. If it is not, the shape is grazing-ambiguous and the binary alternatives come back. Future epochs need wider windows than the linear ephemeris suggests.

Diminishing returns. For all three, further work on existing public data would re-reduce the same photons or re-weight the same scenarios. The remaining alternatives (unresolved companions within about 1-2″, small-radius-ratio diluted pairs, the 270 timing question, and brown dwarfs for 193) need new data. The single smallest observations: for 262, one high-resolution image (AO or speckle reaching Δmag about 6-7 at 0.1-2″); for 193, one resolved multiband transit; for 270, one transit with a wide window (it tests timing and shape together). No observing requests were made.

Failures, negative results and access limits

  • The first replay launch ran its workers at below-normal priority, and they were starved next to the live survey (0-2 CPU-s in 35 min). It was killed and relaunched at normal priority. No result came from the first launch.
  • A neighbour-selection defect (a G-magnitude cut) dropped TIC 193718989's 9.8″ star from the first localization run. It was fixed and rerun; the old outputs are kept as *_run1_Gcut.json.
  • The first Gaia-RV limit used an invalid statistic for pobs near 1. It was replaced by a relative statistic (amendment A2).
  • Timing-null outputs initially overwrote one another. They were rerun per reduction; the stale files are renamed *_STALE_*.
  • The PRF loader first picked up 33×33 “prf-phot” files on camera 4 CCD 2. It was fixed before any result was used.
  • The covariance-weighted image statistic is unstable for some faint hosts (it went negative for one 262 neighbour). The diagonal-error statistic, which the injections calibrate, is the one reported.
  • TGLC's S27 aperture event for TIC 270573718 reads 12 ppt, against 2-4 ppt in every other reduction and −1.4 ppt in TGLC PSF. It is retained in the tables and treated as a TGLC artefact.
  • Unbounded single-source centroid fits wander up to about 100″ in low-S/N sectors. They are diagnostics only.
  • The unbounded free-shape timing fit latched onto outliers in the unclipped pixel series (S1: a 25-ppt, 1.1-h fit at the duration bound). It is reported but not interpreted; a bounded, outlier-clipped variant was added post hoc (A3).
  • The MCMC chains are short (autocorrelation 60-100 steps against 1,000 kept). Medians and 68% ranges are stable; 95% tails are approximate.
  • Access: ExoFOP per-target endpoints return “Array”; the ASAS-SN light-curve service is down; the NASA Exoplanet Archive cone search was blocked (403); ZTF and ATLAS forced photometry are account-gated. None of these is a scientific negative.
  • Negative results kept: every negative or zero event depth (event table); the half-phase nulls; the TIC 262843927 phase-0.387 null; the TIC 262843927 S31/S88 “no information” outcome; the non-significant timing χ² nulls.

Reproduction

Folder: C:\Users\seanj\Documents\TESS_followup_262_193_270 (code, results, tables, figures, manifests, PROTOCOL.md); large caches in D:\tess_fu3_cache (TESScut cutouts, TGLC, PRF models, replay stores and runs). Interpreter: the tesshunter venv (python 3.13.3, numpy 2.5.1, scipy 1.18.0, astropy 8.0.1, batman 2.5.1, emcee 3.1.6, lightkurve 2.6.0).

Order: s00_inventory → s01_270_reproduce, s01b_decompose_all → s02_events → s03_calibrate → s04_oc → s05_tglc → s06_timestamp_control → s07a_cutouts → s07b_extract → s13_fluxbudget → s07c_localize → s09_262_s31_s88 → s10_secondary_2p, s10b_phase0387 → s11_shape → s12_fpp_audit → s14_ztf → s15_rv_limits → s16_ttv_null → s17_mcmc → s18_longp_bls → s19_freeshape_timing (plain and --bounded) → s20_gaia_epochs → s21_spoc2min_262 → s22_cmd_luminosity → s08_replay (select, build, run) → s08b_discovery_context → s08_summarize → facts, build_tables, make_figures → report_body (HTML) → make_pdf → make_manifest. Every script writes JSON under results/ and logs under logs/. Census scripts are under code/census/, with receipts in results/census/receipts/.

Machine-readable tables: tables/event_table_all_reductions.csv (every event in every reduction), pooled_depths, injection_null_calibration, timing_null_tests, model_comparison, host_localization, flux_budget, fpp_scenario_audit, secondary_odd_even, gaia_rv_limits, ztf_193718989, cmd_luminosity, freeshape_timing, discovery_funnel_targets and replay_summary (one row per replay search). Input hashes are in manifests/input_manifest.csv, the protocol hashes in manifests/protocol_freeze.json, the software versions in manifests/environment.json, and the size and SHA-256 of every output file in manifests/output_manifest.csv. A PDF copy of this report is report/FU3_three_candidates.pdf.

Unit tests: code/tests/test_fu3.py, 13 tests on synthetic data (event admission, unbiased depth and timing recovery, pooling, the Gaia-to-TESS magnitude relation, season grouping, the RV mass conversion, the replay's binomial limits and the bounded free-shape fit). Run them with the venv interpreter: python -m pytest code/tests -q.
